newsitem.title: ITALY: GOLF-GOOSEN LEADS AFTER ROMERO GAFFE.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-GOOSEN LEADS AFTER ROMERO GAFFE.

text.p: A moment's carelessness cost Eduardo Romero the chance to share the lead with South African Retief Goosen in the first round of the Italian Open on Thursday.
The veteran Argentine was penalised two strokes for a putting infringement at the 14th and instead of a six-under-par 66 had to settle for a 68.
Goosen defied flu to fire a 66 for a one-shot lead over Welshman Ian Woosnam with Romero joint third in a group of eight which included Spaniard Jose Maria Olazabal.
Romero, 42, unwittingly touched the line of his putt, breaking the tour's local rule, while lining up at the 14th.
He had to be informed of his indiscretion by English playing partners Carl Mason and Jonathan Lomas, who reported the incident to the tournament director.
"On the 14th green, Eduardo walked forward on his line and played a couple of practice swings 10 feet from the cup," tournament director David Garland said.

"His partners noticed he grounded his club, Jon Lomas watching through his legs as he touched his line, although he cannot remember doing so. We had no other proof because the television cameras did not show it, but Eduardo accepted the penalty."

Romero said: "I don't know what happened because I didn't see anything, feel anything. Carl and Jonathan say they both saw it so I accept that. Now I have the determination to win, so no problem. Now I will shoot 66 in the second round."
Goosen's record round for the Gardagolf club of 66 contained an eagle and four birdies.
"The old saying beware the sick golfer was true today," said Goosen, whose maiden European Tour victory came in last year's Slaley Hall Challenge.
"I felt terrible. I guess I felt so ill I just got on with it and I holed some putts."

The 28-year-old South African ran in a 50-foot birdie putt at the last to edge one in front of Woosnam, who said his challenge came from switching back to a wooden driver as he picked up five birdies.
Woosnam said he hooked several drives with the wooden club "but that was okay because it took the right side of the course out of play for me and that's the tough side of the course."
Olazabal had his best day with the driver since he returned from injury in February, four birdies in the last eight holes vaulting him into contention.

The key was a metal driver produced by his own company. "I shocked myself today because I drove really, really well for the first time this year," he said. "The driver has been the weakest club in my bag, but not today.
He likes the Gardagolf. "It's one of the best courses I've played this year and the European Tour should find us more to test us to the full."
He said his ailing feet still hurt a bit "but they are getting better." He will consult his doctor again next week.
